extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, attorneys, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing who may sue or be sued in U.S. patent litigation (standing, assignees, licensees, executors, joint owners), and doctrines of direct, vicarious, joint, and contributory infringement and defenses (including government and public-entity immunity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for Government use of patented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the United States makes or uses specimens of a patented invention without consent, the remedy is provided by statute: after the Act of June 25, 1910 (36 Stat. 851) the Court of Claims has jurisdiction of suits by owners of patents and licensees to recover reasonable compensation for Government use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the 1910 Act there was debate as to remedies because the U.S. cannot be sued except by statute; the Act settled jurisdiction in the Court of Claims for reasonable compensation. The statutory remedy may be different from ordinary injunctive relief; injunctions against the federal government are limited by sovereign immunity and statutory waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability of government officers for unauthorized use
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions existed historically about personal liability of U.S. officers who authorized or were chargeable with unauthorized use of patented inventions, but later law holds that actions do not routinely lie against agents of the Government in such circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is discussed more fully elsewhere (see referenced section). The general rule is that sovereign immunity and evolving precedent limit suits against individual government officers for acts done in official capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be plaintiff in patent infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff/complainant may be the patentee, the sole assignee of the patent, any grantee under the patent (for infringements within his territory), the owner of an equitable title (may sue in equity if defendant is patentee or assignee), partnerships (may sue in partnership name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A partnership is an artificial plaintiff name and may be used. The treatise also notes distinctions between actions at law and equity with respect to required present interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing for actions at law: ownership at time of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: For an action at law it is enough if the plaintiff was the patentee, assignee, or grantee of the rights infringed at the time the infringement sued upon was committed; present ownership at time of suit is not always necessary for legal actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule allows persons who owned the right when the wrongful act occurred to recover at law even if title later changed. By contrast, equitable relief (injunctions) generally requires a present interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity suits and requirement of present interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions in equity (for injunctions) generally require that the complainant have a present interest in the patent; a person with no interest cannot obtain an injunction to restrain future infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exception: if the complainant owned the patent when filing a bill for injunction and money recovery, jurisdiction will not lapse if he assigns the future of his patent after filing. Equity jurisdiction may nonetheless permit suits by assignees in some circumstances (e.g., assignor corporation dissolved, impossible to sue in assignor's name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions by assignees for past infringements and nominal plaintiffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions at law brought by assignees for infringements committed prior to the time they obtained title must, at common law, be brought in the name of the person who held legal title when and where the infringement occurred; an assignee of a mere claim for damages (not of the patent) cannot maintain such a suit in his own name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes permitting assignees to bring suits contemplate assignees of patents (title), not assignees of bare claims for damages. Equity actions may be more flexible, allowing assignees to sue for infringements committed both before and after they obtained title in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor or administrator may sue for deceased patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee entitled to sue dies before beginning an action, an executor or administrator may bring the action, subject to fulfilling conditions and giving guarantees (fidelity, solvency) required by the law of the State where the suit is to be brought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is some conflict in authority as to whether foreign executors/administrators must conform to local probate-like requirements when suing in federal courts of another State. Omitting to comply with such local conditions cannot be asserted by defendant unless pleaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of executor/administrator can sue without local probate if able to sue in own name
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an executor or administrator assigns a patent right or a right of action to another, that assignee can sue in any State without probate proceedings provided he can sue in his own name, which depends on entitlement to injunction/equity or state law permitting assignees of rights of action to sue in their own names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the assignee may sue in his own name turns on whether he is entitled to equitable relief (injunction) or whether equity can take jurisdiction on some other ground; otherwise, state statutes may control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorneys-in-fact and bringing suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees and other persons entitled to bring infringement actions may appoint attorneys in fact to bring those actions in the names of the appointors, but not in the names of the attorneys in fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power-of-attorney may be used so that the suit appears in the appointor's name while the attorney-in-fact prosecutes it; the suit cannot be brought in the agent's own name unless the agent holds title or is otherwise entitled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners in common and requirement of joinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners in common of patent rights must sue jointly for infringement; the defendant may plead in abatement or demur or move to dismiss if necessary parties are not joined. This applies to undivided interests and to partial territorial grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent owner has assigned an undivided part, the action must be brought by patentee and assignee jointly; where territorial divisions exist, multiple owners across territories may join in a suit in one territory. Persons with only an interest in proceeds (no title) need not join.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensees' standing: exclusive vs nonexclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensees under patents generally cannot bring actions for infringement in their own names. Where a person has an exclusive license within a specified territory, actions at law against infringers must be brought in the name of the patent owner but generally for the use of the licensee; equity suits should be brought by owner and exclusive licensee as joint complainants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule applies even when the license is oral or incident to a partnership. Holders of less-than-exclusive licenses may not join in equity suits; exclusive licensees who assign their license generally cannot join in equity suits for past infringements committed before assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive licensee's practical rights to maintain suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions at law begun nominally in the patent owner's name but actually begun by an exclusive licensee may be maintained by the licensee even against the owner's will; an exclusive licensee may bring an equity action in the name of himself and the owner and maintain it without the owner's cooperation or against his objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exclusive licensee may sue to protect his rights; if the owner is himself infringing the exclusive licensee's rights, the licensee may seek equitable relief against the owner. Conversely, exclusive licensee who permits infringement without acting may allow the owner to sue in his own name for his own use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be sued as defendant; public entities and sovereign immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants may be natural persons, partnerships, private corporations, receivers appointed by state courts, trustees in bankruptcy, and assignees for benefit of creditors. Public corporations such as cities and villages are generally liable unless statutes or charters provide otherwise; counties and townships may differ. States cannot be sued for patent infringement without statutory consent, and state officers are not typically liable for state-conducted infringing acts they did not direct or know about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability for public bodies depends on how they were created and the statutes/charters governing them; whether counties or school districts are liable varies by jurisdiction and statute. Individuals cannot avoid liability by showing they supplied infringing goods under contract to a city (personal liability may attach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of minors and married women (historical rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minors are liable for patent infringements (including acts done at father's command). Historically, a married woman committing an infringement in the husband's presence was not liable unless it can be shown she acted without his influence or consent; the husband could be held liable for torts committed in his presence or under his direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules reflect older doctrines of marital status and agency; references to treatise on torts and case law are provided. Modern law may differ; these historic principles may be limited by contemporary statutes and doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of agents, foremen, employees, and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents or salesmen who sell or lease specimens of a patented thing are liable as infringers; foremen supervising infringing activity are liable; any employed person who derives a distinct independent benefit from infringing under direction of employer is liable. Conversely, a mechanic who, while working for wages, makes or uses a patented thing at employer's command is not personally liable in an action at law (though may be enjoined), and an account of profits is not appropriate against such a mechanic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer liability generally coexists (employer is also subject to injunction). The mechanic's lack of liability for profits reflects absence of independent benefit; injunction is the appropriate remedy to restrain further acts. Cases cited distinguish employees who personally profit versus those acting only as paid labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for directing, requesting, approving, or benefiting from infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever directs or requests another to infringe a patent is himself liable for resulting infringement; a person who benefits from an infringement (even if without prior knowledge) and approves it after the fact may be held liable; an employer is liable for infringements committed by employees in the regular course of business even if he forbade the acts or lacked knowledge of their infringing character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows the principle that one who causes or ratifies tortious conduct is responsible. Approval after commission, ratification, or benefit from the infringement are sufficient bases for liability; the employer-employee relationship grounds respondeat superior liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for acts that naturally cause others to infringe (inducing/causing infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general legal principle applies: whoever does an act that naturally causes another to commit a tort is liable for that tort. Examples: making an unauthorized specimen and selling it to a business user can render the seller liable for the user's infringing use; ordering articles that can be made only by infringing a patent can make the merchant liable; commissioning plans and obtaining bids for infringing machinery and receiving compensation makes the planner liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: where a merchant orders articles that may be made with or without a patented process, and manufacturer chooses to use the patented process, the merchant is not liable. Liability turns on foreseeability and whether the act naturally results in infringement or whether the requested product can only be made by infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint liability, contributory liability, and limits on recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several persons cooperate in infringement, all are liable as contributors; they may be sued jointly or singly. Courts will dismiss collusive suits by patentees aimed at advantaging one infringer over another. A suit against several joint infringers may be sustained only against those proved liable; separate acts by individual defendants cannot be aggregated as joint acts to form basis of recovery. Judgments in law suits against joint infringers are entered against all, but only one payment may be enforced; in equity, a decree for profits is entered only against defendants who actually realized profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains procedural consequences (joinder, abatement, demurrer, dismissal for collusion) and equitable limitations on accounting for profits — only those who realized profits from infringement are subject to an account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and rules of contributory infringement (furnishing parts, machines, or specially adapted articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement is intentional aid or cooperation in transactions that collectively constitute complete infringement. Examples: furnishing one part of a patented combination intending it be assembled with other parts and used; furnishing a machine useful only for making a patented article with intent that it be so used; furnishing articles for a patented machine intending they be operated on by it; furnishing a machine or composition particularly adapted to perform a patented process intending that it be so used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The part furnished must be an element of the claimed combination. Sending parts abroad for incorporation may avoid U.S. contributory liability in some cases. If the article or machine has substantial non-infringing uses and the supplier did not intend or know of infringing use, there is no contributory liability; but if the supplier knew or intended the infringing use, he cannot escape liability by showing the property also has non-infringing uses. Case law examples illustrate these distinctions.
